BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Coalition troops on Monday formally handed over security control of Iraq's Anbar province -- once the hub of the country's Sunni insurgency, to Iraqis on Monday. A U.S. soldier on patrol in Ramadi's market earlier this year. U.S. troops will remain in the province to support Iraqi forces. President George W. Bush described the transfer as a major victory against al-Qaeda extremists who once held sway in the area. "Today, Anbar is no longer lost to al Qaeda -- it is al Qaeda that lost Anbar," he said in a statement. Once dominated by Sunni insurgents, Anbar has been the scene of many attacks on U.S.-led troops in Iraq. Now a bastion of tribal opposition, it is also the scene of an internal Sunni political struggle between the Iraqi Islamic Party, one of Iraq's main Sunni parties, and the Awakening movement, the first anti-al Qaeda in Iraq movement established in the country. More than 25,000 U.S. troops serve in the sprawling Anbar province west of Baghdad; most of them Marines. They will remain for the time being but will shift their mission to supporting Iraqi forces, when needed . The transfer is a "major progress" for all of Iraq, said Brigadier Gen. David Perkins, the spokesman for the Multi-National Force in Iraq. The transfer ceremony took place in Ramadi, the capital of the western province, and was attended by Iraqi officials and U.S. military brass.  Watch U.S., Iraqi officials perform transfer » . "We are all well aware of what the security situation was in Anbar even a year ago," Perkins said. "And the fact that that has been able to be turned around, that the Iraqi citizens that live there want to stand up on their own, [that] they want to take control of the province on their own ... it's a major progress not only for Anbar, but for all of Iraq." Anbar is the 11th of Iraq's 18 provinces to revert to local security control, but is the first Sunni-dominated one. The move comes amid a big drop in violence in Iraq and calls from Iraqis for the United States to come up with a troop withdrawal timetable. The other provinces that have transitioned to Iraqi security control are Duhuk, Irbil and Sulaimaniya in the Kurdish region, and Karbala, Najaf, Qadisiya, Muthanna, Thiqar, Basra, and Maysan in the Shiite south. CNN's Jomana Karadsheh and Arwa Damon in Baghdad contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — Coalition troops on Monday formally transferred security control of Iraq’s Anbar province—once the hub of the country’s Sunni insurgency—to Iraqi authorities.

A U.S. soldier was seen on patrol in Ramadi’s market earlier this year. U.S. troops will remain in the province to support Iraqi forces.

President George W. Bush described the transfer as a major victory against al-Qaeda extremists who once held sway in the area.

“Today, Anbar is no longer lost to al Qaeda—it is al Qaeda that lost Anbar,” he said in a statement.

Once dominated by Sunni insurgents, Anbar has been the scene of many attacks on U.S.-led troops in Iraq. Now a bastion of tribal opposition, it is also the site of an internal Sunni political struggle between the Iraqi Islamic Party, one of Iraq’s main Sunni parties, and the Awakening movement, the first anti-al Qaeda in Iraq movement established in the country.

More than 25,000 U.S. troops serve in the sprawling Anbar province west of Baghdad, most of them Marines. They will remain there for the time being but will shift their mission to supporting Iraqi forces when needed.

The transfer represents “major progress” for all of Iraq, said Brig. Gen. David Perkins, spokesman for the Multi-National Force in Iraq.

The transfer ceremony took place in Ramadi, the capital of the western province, and was attended by Iraqi officials and senior U.S. military leaders.

“We are all well aware of what the security situation was in Anbar even a year ago,” Perkins said. “And the fact that that has been able to be turned around, that the Iraqi citizens that live there want to stand up on their own, [that] they want to take control of the province on their own ... it’s a major progress not only for Anbar, but for all of Iraq.”

Anbar is the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to revert to local security control, but the first Sunni-dominated province to do so. The move comes amid a sharp decline in violence in Iraq and growing calls from Iraqis for the United States to establish a timetable for troop withdrawal.

The other provinces that have transitioned to Iraqi security control are Duhuk, Irbil, and Sulaimaniya in the Kurdish region, and Karbala, Najaf, Qadisiya, Muthanna, Thiqar, Basra, and Maysan in the Shiite south.

CNN’s Jomana Karadsheh and Arwa Damon in Baghdad contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — On Monday, coalition forces officially transferred responsibility for security in Iraq’s Anbar province to Iraqi authorities. The province, which had once been the center of the country’s Sunni insurgency, will still have U.S. troops present to assist Iraqi forces when necessary.

Earlier this year, a U.S. soldier was seen patrolling a market in Ramadi. More than 25,000 American service members are stationed across the vast province west of Baghdad, most of them Marines. For now, they will stay in Anbar, but their role will change to one focused on backing up Iraqi security forces as needed.

President George W. Bush called the handover an important success in the fight against al-Qaeda militants, who previously had strong influence in the province.

“Today, Anbar is no longer lost to al Qaeda — it is al Qaeda that lost Anbar,” Bush said in a statement.

Anbar, once controlled heavily by Sunni insurgent groups, had been the site of numerous attacks against U.S.-led forces in Iraq. It has since become a stronghold of tribal resistance to al-Qaeda. At the same time, the province is experiencing a Sunni political rivalry between the Iraqi Islamic Party, one of the country’s leading Sunni political groups, and the Awakening movement, Iraq’s first organized anti-al-Qaeda movement.

Brig. Gen. David Perkins, spokesman for the Multi-National Force in Iraq, said the handover represented “major progress” not just for Anbar but for the entire country.

The ceremony marking the transfer was held in Ramadi, the capital of the western province, with Iraqi officials and senior U.S. military officers in attendance.

“We are all well aware of what the security situation was in Anbar even a year ago,” Perkins said. He added that the improvement, along with the desire of Anbar’s residents to take responsibility for their own province, marked significant progress for both Anbar and Iraq as a whole.

Anbar is the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to return to Iraqi security control, and it is the first Sunni-majority province to do so. The handover comes as violence in Iraq has fallen sharply and as Iraqis have increasingly urged the United States to set a timetable for withdrawing troops.

The other provinces already transferred to Iraqi security authority are Duhuk, Irbil and Sulaimaniya in the Kurdish region, along with Karbala, Najaf, Qadisiya, Muthanna, Thiqar, Basra and Maysan in the Shiite-majority south.

CNN’s Jomana Karadsheh and Arwa Damon in Baghdad contributed to this report.

President George W. Bush described the handover as a major victory against al-Qaeda extremists, particularly because Anbar had once been one of the strongest centers of the Sunni insurgency. The province, located west of Baghdad and stretching to the borders with Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, had been the scene of some of the fiercest fighting of the Iraq war.

Although Iraqi forces will now take the lead in maintaining security, more than 25,000 U.S. troops, most of them Marines, will remain in Anbar. Their mission will shift from direct combat operations to a supporting role, including training, advising, and assisting Iraqi security forces when needed.

U.S. military officials said the transfer reflected major improvements in security not only in Anbar but also across Iraq. They pointed to the decline in violence, the strengthening of Iraqi police and army units, and the cooperation of local Sunni tribes who turned against al-Qaeda-linked militants as key factors behind the progress.

Anbar is now the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to return to local security control. It is also the first Sunni-dominated province to do so, making the handover especially symbolic. The transfer represents both a political and military achievement for the Iraqi government as it continues to assume greater responsibility for the country’s security.

Coalition forces formally transferred security responsibility for Iraq’s Anbar province to Iraqi authorities, marking a major milestone in the country’s effort to assume control of its own security. Under the handover, Iraqi army and police units will take the lead in maintaining order across the province, while U.S. forces move into a supporting role, providing assistance, training, and backup when requested.

The transfer was hailed by both U.S. and Iraqi officials as a significant sign of progress in a region that had once been one of the most dangerous areas in Iraq. Anbar, a largely Sunni province west of Baghdad, was previously a major stronghold for al-Qaeda in Iraq and the center of a fierce insurgency against coalition and Iraqi government forces. For years, the province was associated with intense fighting, roadside bombings, and deep instability.

Officials described the handover as evidence that security conditions had improved dramatically and that local forces were increasingly capable of protecting the population. They said the decline of al-Qaeda’s influence in Anbar showed the success of cooperation between Iraqi security forces, coalition troops, and local tribal leaders who turned against extremist groups.

The ceremony also carried political importance. Anbar became the first Sunni-dominated province to be returned to Iraqi security control, a development seen as an important step toward national stability and reconciliation. Iraqi leaders portrayed the transfer as proof that the government was gaining strength and that the country was moving closer to full sovereignty.

For U.S. forces, the change means a reduced frontline role in the province. Instead of leading daily security operations, American troops will focus on advising Iraqi commanders, supporting missions when needed, and helping ensure that gains made in Anbar are preserved. Coalition officials said the transition reflected confidence in the ability of Iraqi forces to manage security on their own.

The handover of Anbar was widely viewed as one of the most important security transitions in Iraq to that point. Once considered a symbol of the insurgency, the province had become a symbol of recovery and of the shifting balance of responsibility from coalition forces to Iraq’s own institutions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about coalition forces handing over security control of Iraq’s Anbar province to Iraqi authorities, including Bush’s reaction and background on the Sunni insurgency.
counterfactuals.output:
**Coalition hands over security control of Iraq’s Anbar province to Iraqi authorities**

**BAGHDAD, Iraq** — Coalition forces on Monday handed over security responsibility for Iraq’s Anbar province to the Iraqi government, marking a major milestone in a region once considered the heart of the Sunni insurgency and one of the most dangerous areas for U.S. troops.

The transfer gives Iraqi police and army units primary responsibility for security across the vast western province, which stretches from the outskirts of Baghdad to Iraq’s borders with Syria, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. U.S. forces will remain in Anbar in a supporting role, providing assistance if requested by Iraqi authorities.

President George W. Bush praised the handover as a sign of progress in Iraq, saying the change reflected both improved security and the growing capability of Iraqi forces.

“Not long ago, Anbar was al Qaeda’s base in Iraq and was considered lost,” Bush said in remarks responding to the transfer. He credited U.S. troops, Iraqi security forces and local tribal leaders with helping turn the province around.

Anbar is the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to be placed under Iraqi security control. The move follows months of declining violence in the province, where Sunni tribal sheikhs turned against al Qaeda in Iraq and began cooperating with U.S. and Iraqi forces in what became known as the “Anbar Awakening.”

For years after the 2003 U.S.-led invasion, Anbar was a center of resistance to coalition forces and Iraq’s Shiite-led government. Cities such as Falluja and Ramadi became synonymous with fierce fighting, roadside bombs and militant attacks. Falluja was the scene of some of the war’s heaviest urban combat in 2004, when U.S. Marines battled insurgents entrenched in the city.

The insurgency in Anbar was fueled by anger among many Sunni Arabs who had dominated Iraq under Saddam Hussein but lost power after his government was toppled. Militant groups, including al Qaeda in Iraq, exploited that resentment, targeting U.S. troops, Iraqi officials and civilians.

But the situation began to shift in 2006 and 2007, when tribal leaders in Anbar — frustrated by al Qaeda’s brutality and attempts to impose strict control — formed alliances with U.S. forces. The movement helped drive militants from many communities and coincided with the U.S. troop “surge,” which put additional American forces into Iraq.

Iraqi officials hailed Monday’s transfer as evidence that the country is moving closer to full sovereignty and stability. Still, U.S. commanders have cautioned that security gains remain fragile, and that political reconciliation, economic development and continued support for local security forces will be crucial to preventing a resurgence of violence.

The handover comes as the United States and Iraq continue negotiations over the future role of American troops in the country. While violence nationwide has dropped sharply from its peak, insurgent attacks and sectarian tensions remain persistent challenges.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**BAGHDAD —** Iraq’s western Anbar province, once the heart of the Sunni insurgency and a stronghold for al-Qaeda in Iraq, was formally transferred from U.S.-led coalition security control to Iraqi authority on Monday, marking a major milestone in the country’s effort to assume responsibility for its own security.

The handover ceremony in the provincial capital, Ramadi, underscored the dramatic shift in Anbar, a vast desert province stretching from the outskirts of Baghdad to the borders with Syria, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. For years, Anbar was among the most dangerous areas in Iraq, the scene of fierce fighting between U.S. forces, insurgents and militants aligned with al-Qaeda.

Iraqi officials hailed the transfer as evidence that local security forces are increasingly capable of maintaining order without direct coalition command. Under the arrangement, Iraqi police and army units will take the lead in security operations, while U.S. troops remain in the province in a supporting role, available for training, logistics and emergency assistance if requested.

The change follows a sharp decline in violence in Anbar, credited in large part to the rise of the Awakening movement, a coalition of Sunni tribal leaders and former insurgents who turned against al-Qaeda and partnered with U.S. forces. The movement began in Anbar and later spread to other parts of Iraq, becoming a key element in efforts to weaken extremist networks.

Ramadi, once the scene of daily attacks and heavy street battles, has seen significant improvements in security, though officials cautioned that threats remain. Iraqi and U.S. commanders said al-Qaeda in Iraq has been severely weakened in the province but not eliminated, and they warned that militants may attempt to exploit political tensions or gaps in local governance.

Anbar is the latest province to be handed over to Iraqi control as part of a broader process of transferring security responsibility from coalition forces to the Iraqi government. The move comes as the United States continues to maintain a large troop presence in Iraq, though U.S. officials have increasingly emphasized advisory and support missions in areas where Iraqi forces have taken the lead.

Iraqi leaders described the transfer as a step toward full sovereignty and a sign of growing confidence in national security institutions. For residents of Anbar, the handover carried particular symbolism: a province once synonymous with insurgency is now being presented as a model for stabilization.

Still, challenges remain. Local leaders have pressed Baghdad to integrate Awakening fighters into the security forces or provide them with government jobs, warning that failure to do so could create resentment and instability. Reconstruction, unemployment and political representation also remain major concerns in the province.

U.S. officials said coalition forces would continue working with Iraqi authorities in Anbar, but stressed that security decisions now rest primarily with the Iraqi government. The transfer, they said, reflects both improved conditions on the ground and the changing role of American forces as Iraq moves toward greater control over its territory.

counterfactuals.output:
**Iraqi Forces Take Control of Anbar Province in Symbolic Ramadi Ceremony**

**RAMADI, Iraq —** In a ceremony rich with symbolism and political weight, U.S.-led coalition forces formally transferred responsibility for security in Anbar province to Iraqi authorities, marking a dramatic turnabout in a region once regarded as the heartland of the Sunni insurgency and one of the most dangerous battlefields of the Iraq War.

The handover, held in the provincial capital of Ramadi, made Anbar the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to come under Iraqi security control. Iraqi officials hailed the transfer as proof that the country’s army and police are increasingly capable of maintaining order, while U.S. commanders described it as one of the clearest signs yet that violence has sharply declined in areas that were once nearly beyond government reach.

“This is a day of victory for Iraq and for the people of Anbar,” Iraqi officials said during the ceremony, attended by provincial leaders, tribal sheikhs, Iraqi security commanders and senior coalition officers. Iraqi flags were raised as responsibility for day-to-day security passed from coalition troops to Iraqi forces.

For years, Anbar was synonymous with the fiercest fighting of the war. The vast western province, stretching from the outskirts of Baghdad to the borders with Syria, Jordan and Saudi Arabia, became a base for Sunni insurgent groups and al-Qaida in Iraq after the 2003 U.S.-led invasion. Cities such as Fallujah and Ramadi saw some of the most intense combat of the conflict, and U.S. Marines suffered heavy casualties in repeated campaigns to wrest control from militants.

The transfer in Ramadi underscored how much the security picture has changed. Violence in Anbar has fallen steeply from its peak, a shift attributed to several factors: the U.S. troop “surge,” a more aggressive counterinsurgency strategy, the growth of Iraqi security forces and, most crucially, the Anbar Awakening — the movement of Sunni tribal leaders who turned against al-Qaida and began cooperating with U.S. forces.

Those tribal fighters, many later incorporated into local security structures or paid as “Sons of Iraq,” helped drive militants out of towns and rural areas where they had once operated openly. Their cooperation with the Iraqi government, however, remains politically sensitive. Many Sunni leaders in Anbar have pressed Baghdad to provide jobs, political inclusion and guarantees that former insurgents or tribal fighters will not be marginalized by the Shiite-led central government.

The handover therefore carried significance beyond the battlefield. It came as Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s government sought to project national authority and sovereignty, while also negotiating the future role of American forces in Iraq. The transfer supported Baghdad’s argument that Iraqi forces were ready to assume greater responsibility, even as U.S. troops remained available for backup, training and logistical support.

Under the arrangement, Iraqi police and army units will take the lead in security operations across Anbar, while coalition forces will move into a supporting role. U.S. troops are not leaving the province immediately; they will continue to assist Iraqi forces if requested and will retain the ability to respond to major threats. But the ceremony marked a formal change in command and a public acknowledgment that Iraqi authorities now bear primary responsibility for keeping the peace.

The event also highlighted the political stakes ahead of provincial elections. Sunni participation in earlier political processes had been limited in many areas, including Anbar, where insurgent intimidation and widespread boycotts left local governance weakened. With violence reduced, Sunni political groups and tribal leaders were expected to compete more openly for influence in provincial councils, making Anbar a test case for whether security gains could be converted into stable local politics.

Before Anbar, security responsibility had already been transferred to Iraqi control in 10 provinces:

1. **Muthanna**  
2. **Dhi Qar**  
3. **Najaf**  
4. **Maysan**  
5. **Irbil**  
6. **Dahuk**  
7. **Sulaymaniyah**  
8. **Karbala**  
9. **Basra**  
10. **Qadisiyah**

Anbar’s addition to that list was especially notable because of the province’s violent recent history. Unlike some southern or Kurdish provinces that had been relatively calmer, Anbar had been a central battleground between U.S. forces, Iraqi troops, insurgents and al-Qaida-linked extremists.

Still, officials cautioned that the transfer did not mean the province was free of danger. Insurgent cells remained capable of bombings, assassinations and attacks on police or tribal figures. The durability of the security gains, analysts said, would depend on whether the Iraqi government could maintain trust with Sunni communities, integrate local fighters, strengthen provincial institutions and prevent al-Qaida in Iraq from exploiting political grievances.

For U.S. commanders, the Ramadi ceremony represented one of the most important milestones of the war: a province once described as lost to insurgents was now being handed to Iraqi forces under far calmer conditions. For Iraqi leaders, it was an opportunity to claim progress toward sovereignty and national reconciliation.

But for many residents of Anbar, the meaning was more immediate. After years of car bombs, street battles, curfews and fear, the transfer offered the hope that the province’s hard-won calm might endure — this time under Iraqi control.
